title: Transportation funding and two rezonings approved
subtitle: Hickory Street townhouses, University Avenue tower, new public highways, a Solve the Crisis motion and summer event thanks.
overview: Council released 2024 capital funding for three transportation programs: trail and bikeway implementation, intersection collision review, and signs and pavement markings. The release was approved {{vote:m5}}. The money was already in the 2024-2026 Capital Budget.

Council also approved two rezonings after formal public meetings. One allows a townhouse development at 18 and 20 Hickory Street West {{vote:m6}}. The other permits a mixed-use tower at 20 University Avenue East {{vote:m7}}. In both cases staff supported the site-specific exemptions, and the applicants' representatives said they want to start building quickly.

Council passed by-laws establishing six streets as public highways and putting the Hickory Street rezoning into effect {{vote:m8}}. The mayor tabled a Solve the Crisis Campaign motion on homelessness, mental health and addictions, which returns for consideration on September 16. Council met in closed session on a large public gathering, and the minutes report no decision from it. Members closed with thanks to staff and volunteers for summer community events.
Council also approved the minutes of three June meetings.

decisions.detail: Council released remaining 2024 capital funding for the Trail & Bikeway Master Plan, Intersection Collision Review & Implementation, and Signs & Pavement Marking projects, in amounts set out in the minutes, as approved in the 2024-2026 Capital Budget.
Council approved Zoning By-law Amendment Z-24-11 for 18 and 20 Hickory Street West, allowing a connected townhouse development with site-specific exemptions.
Council approved Zoning By-law Amendment Z-23-03 for 20 University Avenue East, allowing a mixed-use development with site-specific exemptions.

debate: On Hickory Street, a councillor asked whether a lower first-storey height would set a precedent. Staff said the small scale of the project made it acceptable and that later applications would be judged on their own context.

Council asked about parking, walkway safety and bike storage at Hickory Street. Staff said proposed parking exceeds zoning requirements and that provincial rules mean none is required in that area. The applicant's representative said lighting and low traffic would address walkway concerns, and residents would likely keep bikes in their units.

On University Avenue, council asked about geothermal heating. Staff and the applicant's representative said the region rejected it because of contamination left by the site's former use. Air-source heat pumps will provide heating and cooling instead.

Councillors raised the mix of housing and green space at University Avenue. One asked about the all one-bedroom units, and the applicant's representative said other projects include larger units. On limited green space, the applicant's representative said patios and street trees were prioritized, and the site was previously fully paved.

Council asked about traffic safety at Columbia and Regina. Staff said the development adds very little traffic there, and a collision countermeasures report is due in November. Council also asked about driveway width, and staff said the driveway is narrow where it meets the sidewalk.
